title: Sakichi Toyoda Backs His Son's Dream of Cars
text:
Sakichi Toyoda, the son of a carpenter in a farming village near Nagoya, spent his life improving the loom. He watched his mother and the village women weaving by hand and resolved to make their work easier. After decades of experiment, in 1924 he produced the Type G automatic loom, which changed shuttles without stopping and halted itself the moment a thread broke, so that one worker could watch many machines. That idea, a machine that stops when something goes wrong, later became a pillar of the Toyota production system.

His son Kiichiro studied mechanical engineering at Tokyo Imperial University and became fascinated by automobiles, which Japan was then importing from America. In 1929 the British firm Platt Brothers bought the patent rights to the Toyoda loom. According to the company's history, Sakichi gave the proceeds to Kiichiro to develop cars, encouraging him to serve his country through the automobile as he himself had through the loom.

Sakichi died in 1930. Kiichiro set up an automobile department inside the family's loom company in 1933, studied and took apart foreign cars, and built prototypes. In 1937 the department became an independent company, the Toyota Motor Company. The loom maker's son had founded what would one day become one of the largest carmakers in the world.
lesson: A parent's greatest gift can be the freedom and support to pursue a different dream. Blessing a child's new path can carry the family's work further than repeating it.
source: Toyota Motor Corporation, Toyota: A History of the First 50 Years (1988); Toyota 75 Years history
caveat: Sakichi's exact words to Kiichiro come from company tradition, and the share of patent money used for cars is debated.
